holding_summary: A lessor sought to cancel a lease because the lessee's wife received paying Christian Science patients in the dwelling; the court held this was not a violation of a 'dwelling only' use covenant, reasoning the reception of visitors or patients was merely incidental to residential use. In reaching this result the court relied on and extended its own precedent holding that a householder may admit into his home whomever he chooses, including boarders and lodgers, without the home ceasing to be a private dwelling.

quotes.text: A dwelling-house is a place for the accommodation and shelter of human beings, and the householde r may admit into his house whomsoever he pleases even boarders and lodgers; nor does his home thereby cease to be his private dwelling house

We do not see how it can be said that the actions of the defendant detailed above can be construed into making another use of the property; it still remained a dwelling and the receiving of visitors or patients was only incidental.

notes: This case's own facts concern a Christian Science healer's patients, not a lodger/boarder occupancy; characterization left null because no letting-of-rooms arrangement is characterized here. The doctrine quoted from Moreira v. Heckman (case_id 8502118) is the substantively relevant material, cited here as controlling precedent.

holding_summary: A landlord provisionally seized all effects in premises leased to a boarding house keeper for unpaid rent; boarders intervened to recover their own furniture. The court held that boarders are sub-tenants (undertenants) to the extent they occupy rooms in the leased premises and keep their own furniture there, and since these boarders owed the boarding house keeper nothing at the time of seizure, their property was properly released.

quotes.text: Boarders are in a sense sub-tenants, and where the sub-lessee agreed in good faith to pay the rent in advance payment made in accordance with the terms of the contract is riot a payment made in anticipation under the meaning of R. C. C. 2706
A boarder is an undertenant to the extent that he occupies apartments in the leased premises and keeps his own furniture and effects there.

holding_summary: A lessor sought to annul a lease and dispossess a tenant who had taken in boarders, lodgers, and roomers, on the ground the premises were rented only as a dwelling and the arrangement was an unconsented sublease. The court held a householder may admit into her house, on whatever condition she chooses, whomever she will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers, without her home ceasing to be a private dwelling, and further held that renting rooms to friends while the tenant retains overall superintendence of the premises is not a 'sublease' requiring the lessor's written consent.

quotes.text: But certainly a householder may admit into his house, and on whatever condition he chooses, -whomsoever he will, including boarders, lodgers and roomers; nor does his home thereby cease to be his private dwelling.

holding_summary: Plaintiff, a practical nurse, rented a room from Mrs. Agnew (the building's lessee) and was injured when defective stairs collapsed; the courts below found plaintiff was not a subtenant but merely a 'roomer or lodger' in the leased premises, and that this did not violate the lessee's covenant not to sublease. The Supreme Court held the building owner could not, by contract with the lessee, escape ex delicto liability to such a lodger for injuries caused by the owner's neglect to keep the building in repair.

quotes.text: 4. Landlord and tenant <@=>164(5) — Landlord cannot, by contract with lessee, escape obligation arising ex delicto for injuries to roomer of lessee, resulting from collapse of stairs (Civ. Code, arts. 670, 2315, 2322, 2693-2695).

The district court and the Court of Appeal both found that the plaintiff was not a subtenant, but merely a “roomer or lodger” in the leased premises, and that there was no violation of the obligation of Mrs. Agnew “to make no sublease.”

holding_summary: Plaintiff and her husband occupied a hotel room that its registered occupant had turned over to them with the desk clerk's knowledge and consent, without themselves registering. The court held that hotel registration is not essential to guest status: when a registered occupant, with the hotel management's knowledge and consent, turns his room over to another person to whom the clerk delivers the key, that person becomes an accepted guest of the hotel and not a mere licensee.

quotes.text: The fact that such person fails to register, or is not required to register, is immaterial; as the registration , of guests at a hotel is no part of the contract between the hotel proprietor and the guest

when the registered occupant of a room, with the knowledge and consent of the hotel management, turns his room over to another person, and the hotel clerk delivers the key of the room to that person, he becomes an accepted guest of the hotel, and is not a mere licensee.

holding_summary: Plaintiff operated a business of renting furnished rooms in premises leased from defendant, a purpose known to both parties at the time of leasing; when a neighboring hotel's excavation work destroyed the building's usability for that purpose, the court held plaintiff entitled to cancel the lease and be relieved of rent from judicial demand, since the lessor's warranty extends to the tenant's known business purpose. Plaintiff could not additionally recover damages, however, because the disturbance was caused by third parties' tortious acts, for which the lessor was not liable under Civil Code article 2703.

quotes.text: That the said premises were leased to petitioner for the purpose of renting rooms and keeping furnished rooms therein, which fact was well known to the said John Davidson, agent for the said Miss M. L. Egan

holding_summary: Plaintiff sued her deceased brother-in-law's succession for board and lodging she furnished him in her private home from January 1916 to January 1920. The court held the one-year prescription applicable to innkeepers and others who make it a business of lodging the public does not apply where a private householder furnishes board and lodging to a relative out of kindness rather than as a business, so the ten-year prescription governed and her claim was not barred.

quotes.text: Under Article 3534 of the Civil Code prescription .of one year has no application when one through kindness furnishes hoard and lodging to a parent or friend though that person is not an innkeeper.
